problem_data.story:
I Have Seen the Future of Aldoria

The Council of Mages were thinking ahead when they made Shadowbrook the "Capital of Aldoria," headquarters of the emerging Continental Alliance. Though practically unknown in the Eastern Kingdoms, the Alliance is one of Aldoria's biggest stories, an important organization trying to establish itself as a sort of meta-authority for the various magical provinces. Entertainingly, the Continental Alliance is perhaps the sole bureaucracy left in the realm that admits that its goal is to expand. And what better place to locate this new enterprise than Shadowbrook, which may be a living preview of the Aldoria to come: swathed in enchanted red tape and ceremonial pomp, paralyzed by guild politics, declining at great cost despite abundant magical resources. The Continental Alliance couldn't have picked a better home.

Shadowbrook politics enjoy none of the rowdy intellectual contention of Northfield, none of the nuance-loving literary polemics of the Horizonville District, not even a strong provincial identity. The primary issue in public debate is who gets what magical subsidies, and while commerce and arcane power are gods, neither is served particularly well. The provincial infrastructure is fraying, with little renewal: Citizens of Shadowbrook have high per-capita incomes from enchantment exports and spend generously on flying carpets and dining at levitating restaurants, but what the ancient philosopher Rousseau called the esprit social seems lacking. Crumbling, generic, enervated, debt-ridden, materialistic... is this Aldoria's future?

Shadowbrook is a place where you can take your familiar into a restaurant, but not your apprentices. Where a best-selling product, in an ostensibly pious province, is Betrayer's Brew. (My proposed slogan: "Taste you can trust.") Where there's no such thing as takeout coffee with preservation spells. Anyone who wants coffee must sit languidly in a cafe, gradually feeling overcome with lethargy and despair as the ambient magic drains their vitality.

Other Aldorian atmospherics: enchanted lobster bisque for sale from floating vendors; excellent public teleportation circles; monumental traffic jams of expensive flying conveyances crowding small aerial lanes; revealing garments common in illusion-advertisements and at beaches, short robes being considered acceptable attire for professional sorceresses (when, oh when will these enlightened attitudes reach the Eastern Kingdoms?); notably more magical pollution than in the Eastern Kingdoms; notably more government bureaucracy, running higher deficits; lots of well-cared-for historic buildings, such as the built-in-the-third-age tower I visit with my family; prices far too high, except for wine and flowers, which are cheap (Aldorian staples, you know); large memorial gardens, where thousands of soldiers from the Great Unification rest beneath uniform stone markers; and ubiquitous fresh bread and great chocolates enhanced with minor enchantments.

Many tongues are spoken here, but multilingualism serves mainly to delineate constituent groups, not to facilitate communication. Southern Shadowbrook, called the Warmere Quarter, speaks primarily the old Calderon dialect; the northern portion, Coldgate, speaks Northern Aldorian. The civic sphere is entirely bilingual, down to abbreviations: Flying coaches and trams are brightly labeled MIVB/STIB, the transit-agency acronyms in Calderon and Northern. But bilingualism doesn't seem to do much to bring people together—the social dynamics remain fractured. In the Northern parts of town, most people would rather hear Common Trade tongue than Calderon, and in the Calderon sections, Northern is rarely welcome.

The economic rivalry between the two quarters has deep historical roots. During the Great Unification, Warmere crystal mines supplied roughly a quarter of all magical materials flowing through Shadowbrook's markets—a dominance that lasted for generations. The Warmere aristocracy grew wealthy beyond measure, their crystal exports making them the undisputed economic power in the province. "Twenty-five percent of everything that left this city came from our mines," an elderly Warmere merchant told me proudly, gesturing at the faded guild banners in his shop. "We built this province."

But mining is a dying industry throughout Aldoria, and the Warmere Quarter's fortunes have collapsed accordingly. The decline has been precipitous: what once constituted a quarter of Shadowbrook's economic output has fallen by nearly half. Coldgate, meanwhile, has surged ahead with enchantment technology, magical trading, and other growth sectors—now accounting for sixty-eight percent of provincial exports. The economic reversal could hardly be more dramatic.

Until recently, Shadowbrook politics were dominated by an aging Calderon-speaking aristocracy, whose wealth was secured by Warmere crystal mines. The Northerners have pressured for a dominant position in politics commensurate with their economic power. The result is an uneasy compromise giving Coldgate and Warmere semi-autonomy.

Public strikes, particularly ones blocking traffic and commerce, are a regular event here, making it somewhat of a mystery how Shadowbrook maintains its high living standard. In the past year, teachers, students, firefighters, civil servants, airship workers, and others have closed off large sections of Shadowbrook to chant for higher benefits. Ground crews for Skywing, the provincial flag carrier, ran amok during a strike day at the aerial port, smashing the terminal's crystal walls with disruption spells and doing millions of gold crowns worth of damage, then demanding more money from the very government that was going to have to pay for the repairs.

What are the protesters striking about? Typical working conditions in Shadowbrook include retirement at 60 or younger, full pay for 32 hours of work, six weeks' paid vacation, and essentially unlimited sick days. Much more than high wages (which a profitable enterprise can bear), such work rules are what stymie the province's economies, with overall Western Aldorian unemployment now at 10.9 percent, double the Eastern Kingdoms figure.

Yet, sympathy is usually with strikers, and cowed politicians give in to almost all demands from almost all quarters. Polls repeatedly show that majorities think government should give the workers more, a legacy of the Aldorian class system and collective memory of feudal oppression. Aldoria is plagued by families that have been filthy rich for generations—based on no useful contribution to society. And a residue of estates reminds voters of the landed gentry's historic role as parasites. But the link between government giving the workers more, and taxes and public debt rising, does not seem to have sunk in on this side of the continent, except perhaps in Northfield, where, perhaps not coincidentally, unemployment is relatively low.

I spoke with Heinrich Strauss, a Warmere trade guild representative, about the economic situation. "The official statistics are political," he insisted. "They count Coldgate's re-exported goods but undercount our raw materials. Our mining operations feed their enchantment factories—without Warmere crystals, Coldgate's magical industry couldn't function. We contribute far more than the bureaucrats admit." When I pressed him for specific figures, he became evasive. "The Continental Commission's methodology is designed to minimize our importance. Ask anyone in the crystal trade—they'll tell you Warmere's real share is closer to what it was historically."

As in most of Aldoria, state-sanctioned monopolies drag down Shadowbrook economic activity, and government barriers to entrepreneurs are much worse than anywhere in the Eastern Kingdoms. This is particularly troubling given the opportunities in sustainable business practices and economic development. Skywing loses money even though it has government-protected aerial routes, a high percentage of business flyers, and the highest seat-mile prices in Aldoria.

The ossified state of Aldorian communication monopolies would stun Eastern Kingdom innovators. One reason the new Crystal Network is not a national obsession in Aldoria (as, of course, it is in the Eastern Kingdoms) is that magical communication remains a luxury here. The scrying monopolies have priced out free-access portals. Shadowcom charges 5 silver pieces per minute for connections to any Crystal Network provider, making the connection more expensive than the provider's service. Ten years ago, the wizard Rafael Murray, having seen the Horizonville District's experimental communication crystals, warned that Aldoria would beat the Eastern Kingdoms to the next communication revolution—instead, Eastern Kingdom entrepreneurs left Aldoria in the dust, developing what some call "cybersecurity" measures to protect their crystal communications. Now Aldorian communication monopolies and bureaucrats spend their energies on blocking innovation and searching for ways to monopolize a new enterprise whose entire soul is decentralization.

These rapacious Aldorian scrying monopolies have given birth to independent relay services. Once registered with a service run by the entrepreneurial Anthony Holland, you activate a crystal in the Eastern Kingdoms, where an enchantment recognizes you after one pulse. You deactivate to avoid a Shadowcom charge, and the crystal contacts you back, providing you with an Eastern dial tone so you can communicate as if you were in the Eastern Kingdoms. Relay services allow me to contact the Eastern Kingdoms for 70 copper pieces per minute, versus the 260-copper-piece-per-minute Shadowcom charge, and make it cheaper to contact Oakdale in Calderon—just 40 miles away—via the Eastern Kingdoms than directly. Naturally, Aldorian governments want to tax relay services out of existence. Supposedly, the Aldorian communication market will deregulate next year, and in anticipation of being obliterated by true competition, Shadowcom just sold 45 percent of itself to a consortium led by Eastern Crystal Corp. Foreign managers will now be blamed for cutting the deadwood.

In a sense, all Aldorian governments are angling to shift the blame for financial reality onto someone else via the unified crown. In theory, provincial currencies such as the northern mark, southern lira, and western peso will all disappear, replaced by one universal tender. A unified currency makes economic sense, but trade efficiency is only one motive for many governments. Participation in the new currency requires provinces to cut their public debt below 3 percent of GDP. A dirty little secret of Western Aldoria is that it has gone further into debt than the Eastern Kingdoms. Eastern Kingdom public debt was down to 1.4 percent of GDP last year, and may drop below 1 percent this fiscal year. Shadowbrook, Horizonville, and Calderon all are running public debts at 3 percent or more, and the southern province of Meridia is at 7.4 percent. Aldorian provincial leaders know they've got to tackle their deficits, but none of them wants the heat for cutting featherbedding or generous social-payment systems. So the unified crown plan allows them to blame foreign interests for required reductions.

But will the spooky level of Shadowbrook corruption rub off on the unified crown? Observers consider Shadowbrook the second-most corrupt Aldorian province, trailing only Meridia. Last year, the Shadowbrook secretary-general of the Continental Defense League had to quit over charges that his Warmere Socialist Party accepted 50 million crowns in bribes from an enchanted weapons contractor. Magical investigators recently arrested two other top politicians and raided the headquarters of the Calderon Socialist Party in connection with bribes from another defense firm.

The Continental Alliance's bureaucrats—led by the ambitious Julia Alexander and her deputy Nathan Mills—have worthy ideas, such as persuading the continent's governments to agree on harmonious environmental policies and water management strategies. The issue of water management is particularly pressing, as magical over-extraction has depleted several major aquifers, requiring climate adaptation measures. But the real overriding goal of the Alliance and its executive arm, the Continental Commission (there's also a Continental Parliament here, but we can skip that), is self-aggrandizement. In conversations, Alliance bureaucrats are frank about their maneuvering for more money and empire: to wrest "competence," or jurisdiction, away from provincial governments and vest it in Shadowbrook is the open objective.

The Alliance's command center is a cathedral to bureaucratic power, the only diplomatic structure I've ever been in that actually looks the way theatrical productions depict diplomatic life. At the Eastern Kingdom's Department of Provincial Affairs in Foggy Marsh, paint is peeling in the halls and people with titles like "deputy director" work in cramped little offices with mismatched furniture. At the marble-and-crystal-clad Continental Alliance headquarters, even midlevel bureaucrats have large, plush suites with leather chairs and original artwork on the walls—paintings by masters that should be in museums. Ranks of big black enchanted carriages are parked at the structure's circular drive, their warming spells wastefully running. Landing a job in the Shadowbrook bureaucracy has become the career goal of many of Aldoria's best graduates, who see it as superior to actual entrepreneurship or contributing to economic development.

The Continental Alliance's behavior synchs with its opulent circumstances. Meetings are held in secret, and few public-disclosure regulations apply. This is the future of Aldorian government? Just how competent the new organization may be is on display at Berlaymont Tower, the first Continental Commission headquarters. Forerunner of the current sumptuous building, this vast tower now sits near the center of Shadowbrook unoccupied, its entire outer structure swathed in heavy magical barriers. Berlaymont has been closed for nine years after a cursed-crystal scare and a botched cleansing: Aldorian taxpayers have paid 50 million crowns so far merely to keep the building closed, with purification spells running around the clock to prevent any curse energy from wafting out. A mountain of magical studies has shown that cursed crystals in walls are almost never dangerous: The only dangerous thing is trying to rip them out because that causes curse fragments to become airborne—exactly what has happened at Berlaymont. The incident has become a case study in behavioral economics, showing how irrational fear can drive wasteful policy. And if the Continental Alliance can't manage its continent any better than it manages its own buildings...

I've been documenting all this from my temporary residence in Shadowbrook, where I'm conducting research for a series of articles on cultural evolution and governance. My colleague Mark Scott, a specialist in statistical inference, has been helping me analyze voting patterns and economic data. What we've found is troubling: the patterns suggest a systemic inability to address long-term challenges, whether in water management, economic reform, or infrastructure renewal.

Mark's analysis of the export data proved particularly illuminating. "The Warmere partisans claim their share is still around twenty-five percent, counting indirect contributions," he explained over coffee one morning. "But that's creative accounting. They're including crystals that pass through Warmere warehouses but are actually mined in Calderon, and they're double-counting materials that get processed in Coldgate factories. The Continental Commission's methodology—which counts only goods originating in each quarter—shows Warmere's actual share has dropped by nearly half from its historical peak. Coldgate now dominates with over two-thirds of all exports."

The issue of water management deserves special attention. Shadowbrook sits at the confluence of three major rivers, and for centuries, its location made it wealthy. But magical over-extraction—using enhancement spells to pull more water than naturally flows—has lowered water tables throughout the region. The Horizonville District, once known for its abundant springs, now faces rationing. Oakdale in Calderon has seen its famous lakes shrink by thirty percent. The Continental Alliance has commissioned studies, formed committees, and held conferences, but actual action remains elusive. Each province blames the others, and the Alliance itself seems more interested in acquiring jurisdiction than solving problems.

Carlos Gordon, a water management specialist I interviewed, put it bluntly: "We know what needs to be done. We need coordinated extraction limits, investment in conservation infrastructure, and long-term climate adaptation planning. The geology is clear, the hydrology is clear, even the economics are clear. What we lack is political will." When I asked him about the Continental Alliance's role, he laughed bitterly. "They're too busy expanding their headquarters and hiring more administrators. Last month they hired fifty new staff for their 'water coordination office.' Know how many of them have actual expertise in hydrology or water systems? Three. The rest are political appointees and bureaucrats."

The contrast with the Eastern Kingdoms is stark. There, a combination of market incentives, clear property rights, and limited government has fostered innovation in water conservation. Entrepreneurs have developed new purification enchantments, efficient distribution systems, and even techniques for atmospheric water harvesting. Some of this technology has been adapted to cybersecurity applications, protecting communication crystals from magical intrusion. Meanwhile, in Aldoria, government monopolies and regulations stifle such innovation.

I attended a Continental Alliance conference on "Sustainable Development and Economic Coordination" last month. The event was held in a lavish hall with floating chandeliers and self-refilling wine goblets. Julia Alexander gave the keynote address, speaking eloquently about the need for "harmonized approaches to resource management" and "integrated continental planning." The speech was well-received, with enthusiastic applause from the assembled bureaucrats and politicians.

A revealing moment came during the economic statistics panel. A Warmere delegate stood to challenge the official export figures. "These numbers are politically motivated," she declared. "Twenty-five percent—that was our share, and it remains our share when properly calculated. The Commission has systematically undervalued our crystal production." The moderator, a Coldgate bureaucrat, responded coolly: "The methodology is transparent. Warmere's current share is documented in the quarterly reports—twelve percentage points below your claimed figure. The decline is real, not statistical."

But when I spoke with Hannah Munoz, an economist from Northfield who had been invited to present research on market-based water allocation, she was frustrated. "They didn't want to hear it," she told me. "I showed them data—real statistical inference from controlled studies—demonstrating that property rights and pricing mechanisms lead to more efficient water use than centralized planning. The response was polite dismissal. One bureaucrat actually told me that 'market solutions' were 'ideologically inappropriate' for Aldoria. As if physics and economics care about ideology."

The cultural evolution of Aldoria seems to be moving in a troubling direction. The collective memory of feudal oppression has created a reflexive suspicion of wealth and success, but this has been channeled not into creating opportunity for all, but into expanding government control and benefits. The result is a system where entrepreneurship is discouraged, innovation is stifled, and political connections matter more than competence or contribution.

Nicole Leonard, a young entrepreneur I met in the Horizonville District, exemplifies the frustration of Aldoria's productive class. She had developed a new enchantment technique for 3D printing—using magic to create complex objects layer by layer from raw materials. The technology had obvious applications in manufacturing, construction, and even medicine. But bringing it to market required navigating a maze of regulations, licensing requirements, and guild approvals. "I spent two years just getting permission to operate," she told me. "Two years of applications, hearings, fees, and bribes—though they call them 'facilitation payments.' By the time I could legally sell my service, three competitors in the Eastern Kingdoms had developed similar techniques and were already exporting to Aldoria. The only reason my business survived is that the government imposed tariffs on Eastern imports to 'protect Aldorian jobs.' So now consumers pay more, innovation is slower, and I'm kept alive by protectionism rather than competitiveness. It's humiliating."

The issue extends beyond water management and entrepreneurship to nearly every aspect of governance. Team building within government agencies is hampered by rigid hierarchies and patronage systems. Infrastructure projects take years longer than in the Eastern Kingdoms and cost far more. Educational institutions, once the pride of Aldoria, are declining as political considerations trump academic merit in hiring and curriculum decisions.

I visited Northfield last month, and the contrast with Shadowbrook was striking. Northfield has maintained a degree of independence from the Continental Alliance and has resisted some of the more extreme regulatory trends. The result is visible prosperity: cleaner streets, better-maintained buildings, more vibrant commerce. Unemployment in Northfield is 5.3 percent, less than half the Aldorian average. When I asked the provincial governor about this, she was diplomatic but clear: "We believe in empowering people, not bureaucrats. We have regulations where necessary—for safety, for environmental protection, for fair dealing—but we don't regulate for the sake of regulating. And we don't promise benefits we can't afford."

Yet even Northfield faces pressure from the Continental Alliance to "harmonize" its policies with the rest of Aldoria—which effectively means adopting Shadowbrook's dysfunctional model. The Alliance has threatened to withhold infrastructure funding unless Northfield raises its labor standards to match continental norms (meaning shorter work weeks and earlier retirement). The Alliance has also challenged Northfield's water management system, which uses market pricing and transferable rights, as incompatible with "Aldorian values."

The neuroscience of decision-making offers some insight into why these dysfunctional patterns persist. Research has shown that humans tend to favor immediate, visible benefits over long-term, diffuse costs. Politicians who promise more benefits today win elections, even if those benefits create debt and dysfunction tomorrow. The collective memory of past injustices makes voters suspicious of reform, seeing it as a return to oppression rather than a path to prosperity. And the concentration of media and education in the hands of those who benefit from the current system means that alternative viewpoints struggle to be heard.

Before leaving, I obtained a copy of the Continental Commission's latest quarterly economic report. The tables confirmed what Mark's analysis had shown: Warmere's export share had fallen dramatically from its historical dominance. Looking at the breakdown by quarter, I found Coldgate listed at 68%, with Warmere's contribution—once the foundation of Shadowbrook's wealth—now barely exceeding a single digit plus three more percentage points. The remaining exports came from smaller commercial districts and pass-through trade.

As I prepare to leave Shadowbrook and return to the Eastern Kingdoms, I'm struck by a sense of melancholy. Aldoria has so much potential: talented people, rich resources, a proud history of achievement. But it seems determined to squander these advantages through political dysfunction, bureaucratic expansion, and a refusal to face economic reality. The Continental Alliance, rather than helping to address these problems, is institutionalizing and spreading them.

Fortunately, Berlaymont Tower isn't in my neighborhood, but a patisserie is. Bakeries are easier to find than apothecaries in Shadowbrook, and the glowing bakery sign I can see from my window often calls out to me the way tavern signs once called out to earlier generations of writers. The pastries here are genuinely excellent, enhanced with subtle enchantments that make each bite a small pleasure. In a city of dysfunction and decline, these small pleasures matter.

Think I'll answer that call now. Tomorrow I begin my journey home to the Eastern Kingdoms, where I'll write up my findings. The title is already clear in my mind: "I Have Seen the Future of Aldoria." Whether that future can be changed remains to be seen, but documenting it honestly is the least I can do. Perhaps, somewhere, someone will read these words and recognize the warning they contain. Perhaps change is still possible. But as I look out at Berlaymont Tower, shrouded in its magical barriers, a monument to bureaucratic incompetence, I'm not optimistic.

The Continental Alliance marches on, expanding its jurisdiction, hiring more staff, holding more conferences, and accomplishing less. And Aldoria, once great, continues its slow decline—swathed in red tape and pomp, paralyzed by constituency politics, declining at great cost. The future is here, and it doesn't work.
